opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that when you build the agent and the model together, you're not limited to the model's current behavior. You can actually change it.

If you're a third-party developer, the model is a fixed black box. You study how it behaves, where it's strong, where it fails, and then you write prompts, workflows, and scaffolding around those properties. That can work very well in the short term, and many great products have been built this way. But your ceiling is basically the model's existing capability plus how cleverly you can engineer around its weaknesses. A lot of that engineering is compensating for things the model can't do yet, and much of it becomes obsolete when the next model comes out.

When the model company builds the agent, the loop is different. You see where the agent fails in real tasks, and instead of adding another rule to the workflow, you can go back into training: build environments for those tasks, collect the trajectories, do reinforcement learning on the actual end-to-end behavior. So the product isn't just a wrapper anymore. The product experience feeds directly into the model's capabilities. That's a much more scalable way to improve, because you're improving the underlying intelligence rather than patching symptoms.

There's also a deeper point. With agents, the boundary between "model" and "product" is getting blurry. Things like how to use tools, how to plan over long horizons, how to recover from errors, when to ask the user for clarification: these used to be product logic, and now they're increasingly behaviors you train into the model. If you can only reverse-engineer, you're always one step behind, adapting to whatever the model happens to do. If you own the training, you can decide what the model *should* do and make it happen.

So I'd say reverse-engineering gives you a local optimum, which can be quite good. Co-designing model and agent gives you a path to keep raising the ceiling, because every product insight can become a training signal. And over time, I think that compounding effect is what matters most.

r002.rationale: It says training on real tasks and end-to-end behavior lets product experience improve the model’s capabilities, supporting better performance in that environment.

r003.rationale: The response proposes addressing failures through training and describes tool use as a behavior to train; it does not identify adjusting tool design as a remedy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that the model and the product are not really two separate things anymore. When you build an agent on top of someone else's model, you are essentially observing its behavior from the outside, finding where it works and where it breaks, and then wrapping a lot of scaffolding around it to compensate. You can get quite far that way, but you are always constrained by what the model already is. If the model can't do something, you have to fake it with prompts or workflows, and that is fragile.

When you are the model company, you can go the other direction. You see what users are actually trying to do with the agent, where it fails, where it hesitates, where it loses track of a long task, and you can take that signal straight back into training. The product becomes the environment for the model, and the model becomes the core of the product. That loop is the real advantage. Every failure in the product is a training target, and every improvement in the model shows up in the product without someone having to re-engineer the scaffolding.

There is also a deeper point about where capability actually lives. A lot of what makes an agent good, things like knowing when to use a tool, when to stop and check, how to recover from an error, how to maintain a plan over hundreds of steps, these are not really product features. They are model capabilities. You can approximate them with external logic, but the approximation has a ceiling, and that ceiling is set by the person who trained the model, not the person who wrapped it. If you can push those behaviors into the weights, the ceiling rises with every training run.

So I would put it this way. Reverse-engineering a model's behavior gives you a product that is as good as the model today. Building the model and the product together gives you a product that can become as good as the model can be. Over a long enough horizon, that second curve wins, because the first one is bounded by someone else's decisions and the second one is bounded only by how fast you can learn from your own users.

r001.rationale: The response says the product becomes the model’s environment, but does not say that the tool environment is designed before training the model in it.

r002.rationale: It describes sending product failures back into training, but does not clearly state that training in the intended environment naturally improves performance in that environment.

r003.rationale: The response discusses improving model capabilities through training and using scaffolding, but does not identify adjusting tool design as a way to address difficulties.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether you can improve the model and the product together. If you’re building on someone else’s model, you observe its behavior and then design prompts, tools, and workflows around it. You can build a very good product that way, but when you hit a limitation in the model, you mostly have to work around it.

A model company has another option: change the model. If an agent struggles with a particular kind of task, you can use that failure to guide training, improve how it uses tools, and then adjust the product around those new capabilities. The model and the agent can evolve together.

That’s why I think the ceiling can be higher. It doesn’t mean the first-party product automatically wins—you still need good product judgment and execution. But you have a broader set of things you can optimize, rather than treating the model as something fixed.

r001.rationale: The response describes improving the model and product together, but does not say to design the tool environment before training the model within it.

r002.rationale: It says failures can guide training and tool-use improvements, but does not state that training the model in the intended product environment naturally improves its performance there.

r003.rationale: It mentions improving tool use and adjusting the product, but does not clearly identify adjusting tool design as a way to address difficulties the model encounters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the model and the product can evolve together. If you’re building on top of a model from the outside, you observe its behavior, figure out what it’s good at, and then design prompts and workflows around that. You can build a very good product that way, but you’re largely adapting to a capability that’s already there.

If you also train the model, you can work in both directions. You can ask, “What would make this agent experience better?” and then change the model’s training to support that behavior. Maybe it needs to use tools more reliably, recover from mistakes, or stay on task over a longer sequence of actions. Those become model-training problems as well as product-design problems.

That creates a feedback loop: the product reveals where the model fails, and improvements to the model make new product experiences possible. So I wouldn’t say a first-party product automatically wins. Execution still matters. But the ceiling can be higher because you’re optimizing the whole system, rather than only the layer around the model.

r002.rationale: It says training can be changed to support agent behavior, but does not state that training the model in its intended environment naturally improves performance there.

r003.rationale: It mentions making tool use more reliable as a training goal, but does not identify adjusting tool design to address difficulties the model encounters.
